title: Grammar Map · All 15 patterns in one listen (Domum īre volō!)
summary: A one-off: the gist of all fifteen Latin patterns from the app's Forms > Patterns ladder, one focus pyramid each. Who (quī), when (cum, ubi, postquam), because, if / unless, although, says that, so that (ut / nē), asking and ordering, the participle, the ablative absolute, cum + subjunctive, the hidden question, result, the gerund, and -ndum est. The world: a small boy who wants to go home, and his dad. Then the whole map in one story, and the Latin alone twice. Iulia's voice.
lines: {Salvē!} This is a special episode. The Grammar Map. All fifteen patterns in one listen. Just the gist of each, with one focus idea.
Our world today: a small boy who wants things, and his dad. I am the dad. The boy is my son, {fīlius meus}.
First, the whinge kit. Short lines a small child says all day long.
And the king of all whinges.
Remember that one. It will come back again and again. Now the fifteen patterns.
Pattern one. Who and which. {Quī} adds a mini-sentence about a noun.
The boy who is crying is my son.
Puer quī plōrat fīlius meus est.
The boy who wants to go home...
The boy who wants to go home is my son.
Puer quī domum īre vult fīlius meus est.
Spot it: a noun, then {quī}, {quae} or {quod}. Read: who, or which. Careful: {quod} can also mean because.
Puer quī plōrat fīlius meus est.
The boy who is crying is my son.
Pattern two. When. {Cum}, {ubi} and {postquam} tell you when something happens.
We stop playing. My son cries.
When we stop playing, my son cries.
Cum lūdere dēsinimus, fīlius meus plōrat.
When we come to the park...
When we come to the park, he wants to go home.
Ubi in hortum venīmus, domum īre vult.
After we came home, he wanted to go to the park again.
Postquam domum vēnimus, iterum in hortum īre voluit.
Spot it: {cum}, {ubi} or {postquam}, a mini-sentence, then a comma.
Ubi in hortum venīmus, domum īre vult.
When we come to the park, he wants to go home.
Pattern three. Because. {Quod} or {quia} gives the reason.
I am crying because I want to go home!
I am crying because I don't have a biscuit!
My son is crying because he does not have a biscuit.
Fīlius meus plōrat quia crustulum nōn habet.
Spot it: {quod} or {quia} plus a normal verb. Read: because.
I am crying because I want to go home!
Pattern four. If and unless. {Sī} means if. {Nisi} means unless.
You give me a biscuit. I don't cry.
If you give me a biscuit, I don't cry.
Sī mihi crustulum dās, nōn plōrō.
Unless you give me a biscuit...
Unless you give me a biscuit, I cry!
Unless we go home, I cry!
Spot it: {sī} or {nisi} at the start, a comma after the mini-sentence.
Unless you give me a biscuit, I cry!
Pattern five. Although. {Quamquam}, and often {tamen}: still.
We are playing in the park.
Although we are playing in the park...
Although we are playing in the park, he wants to go home.
Quamquam in hortō lūdimus, domum īre vult.
Although we are playing in the park, he still wants to go home.
Quamquam in hortō lūdimus, tamen domum īre vult.
Although he is tired, he still does not want to sleep.
Quamquam fessus est, tamen dormīre nōn vult.
Spot it: {quamquam} at the start, often {tamen} after.
Quamquam in hortō lūdimus, tamen domum īre vult.
Although we are playing in the park, he still wants to go home.
Pattern six. Says that. No word for that. The person goes into the object form, the verb into the infinitive.
My son says that he wants to go home.
Fīlius meus dīcit sē domum īre velle.
My son says that I have...
My son says that I have more biscuits.
Fīlius meus dīcit mē plūs crustulōrum habēre.
I say that this is not true.
{Vult} became {velle}. {Habeō} became {habēre}. Spot it: a say verb, the object form, an infinitive. Read: that.
Fīlius meus dīcit mē plūs crustulōrum habēre.
My son says that I have more biscuits.
Pattern seven. So that. {Ut}, and for so that not, {nē}. The verb takes the swapped form: {audit} becomes {audiat}.
He shouts so that I hear.
He shouts so that everyone hears.
I whisper so that he does not hear me.
Spot it: {ut} or {nē}, then the swapped verb. Read: so that, or so that not.
He shouts so that everyone hears.
Pattern eight. Asking and ordering. After ask, beg or order: {ut} means to, {nē} means not to.
My son begs me for us to go home.
Fīlius meus mē ōrat ut domum eāmus.
I order my son to sleep.
I ask my son not to shout.
Spot it: an order or ask verb, a person, then {ut} or {nē}. Read: to, or not to.
I order my son to sleep.
Pattern nine. The participle. A verb used like a describing word. Like {plōrāns}: crying, at the same time as the main verb. You'll meet this properly later.
My son cries. He calls me.
My son, crying, shouts: I want to go home!
Fīlius meus plōrāns clāmat: Domum īre volō!
Shouting, he runs to the gate.
Spot it: a verb like {plōrāns} or {clāmāns} next to a person. Read: while doing it.

Pattern ten. The ablative absolute. A little side scene, set apart: with this happening, that happens. Both words go into the with-form. The verb word often ends like {cadente}. You'll meet this properly later.
I am sleeping. My son plays.
While I am sleeping, my son plays.
With the sun setting, we go home.
With the sun setting, we finally go home.
Spot it: two words at the start, set off by a comma, like {sōle cadente}. Read: while, or with.
With the sun setting, we finally go home.

Pattern eleven. {Cum} in a past story, with a new verb form: when, or since. It looks like the whole infinitive plus an ending. {Esse} becomes {esset}. {Nōlle} becomes {nōllet}. You'll meet this properly later.
We were in the park. He wanted to go home.
In hortō erāmus. Domum īre volēbat.
When we were in the park, he wanted to go home.
Cum in hortō essēmus, domum īre volēbat.
Since he did not want to sleep...
Since he did not want to sleep, he was crying.
Since he did not want to sleep, he was crying all night.
Cum dormīre nōllet, tōtam noctem plōrābat.
Spot it: {cum} plus a verb built on the infinitive, like {esset}. Read: when, or since, in a story.
Since he did not want to sleep, he was crying.
Pattern twelve. The hidden question. A question inside a sentence. Its verb takes the swapped form.
Why does he want to go home?
I don't know why he wants to go home.
I ask why he is crying.
He does not know why he is crying.
{Vult} became {velit}. {Plōrat} became {plōret}. Spot it: know or ask, then a question word, then a swapped verb.
I don't know why he wants to go home.
Pattern thirteen. Result. So much that. Look for {tam} or {ita} first, then {ut}.
He cries so hard that we go home.
Tam vehementer plōrat ut domum eāmus.
He shouts so hard that everyone looks at us.
Tam vehementer clāmat ut omnēs nōs spectent.
He is so tired that he sleeps in the car.
Tam fessus est ut in raedā dormiat.
Spot it: {tam} or {ita} early, then {ut}. Read: so much that. No {tam} or {ita}? Then {ut} usually means so that, or to.
Tam vehementer plōrat ut domum eāmus.
He cries so hard that we go home.
Pattern fourteen. The gerund. A verb used like a noun: playing, sleeping. {Lūdendī}: of playing. You'll meet this properly later.
My son is keen on playing.
My son is not keen on sleeping.
Fīlius meus nōn cupidus dormiendī est.
Spot it: a word like {lūdendī} or {dormiendī} after time or keen. Read: of doing it.
My son is keen on playing.
Pattern fifteen. Must. {Dormiendum est}: sleeping must be done. Short, strong, and very useful.
Two ways to say must. {Dēbēs}, an ordinary verb. And {eundum est}: it has to be done. Who does it? The story tells you.
The whole map, in one short story. Fifteen patterns.
The boy who is crying is my son.
Puer quī plōrat fīlius meus est.
When we come to the park, he wants to go home.
Ubi in hortum venīmus, domum īre vult.
He cries because he wants to go home.
Unless we go home, he cries.
Although we are playing, he still wants to go home.
Quamquam lūdimus, tamen domum īre vult.
He says that I have more biscuits.
He shouts so that everyone hears.
He begs me for us to go home.
I don't know why he wants to go home.
He shouts so hard that everyone looks at us.
Tam vehementer clāmat ut omnēs nōs spectent.
With the sun setting, we finally go home.
At home he is keen on playing.
And at home, what does he say?
I want to go to the park!
Last night, since he did not want to sleep, he was crying.
So tonight, Dad says the last line.
That is the map. Fifteen patterns. You don't need them all yet. Now you know the shape of each one. {Valē!} Now the Latin alone, twice.
